claims.text: High-temperature structural and chemical stability in high-entropy nanoalloys is governed by formation of a secondary buffering sublattice.
A buffering sublattice accommodates inherent local lattice distortions.
A buffering sublattice reduces local atomic displacements.
A buffering sublattice restricts fast diffusion of unstable species.
Restricted diffusion caused by the buffering sublattice prevents phase segregation and decomposition.
The initial nanoalloy has a homogeneous distribution of multiple metal species.
Some elements in the initial nanoalloy are intrinsically less stable at high temperatures.
A minor alloying or oxide addition can be used to promote an ordered interstitial buffering phase in a high-entropy nanoalloy.
An oxygen sublattice can act as a buffer layer in a rocksalt high-entropy oxide.
The oxygen-sublattice behavior in high-entropy oxides is an appropriate analogue for an engineered buffering sublattice in high-entropy nanoalloys.
The buffering sublattice mitigates rapid cation diffusion.
Accommodation of lattice distortion and suppression of atomic migration delay nucleation of secondary phases.
Accommodation of lattice distortion and suppression of atomic migration delay grain coarsening at high temperature.
Relative to a control without the engineered buffer, a buffered nanoalloy will have a reduced rate of phase segregation after high-temperature exposure.
Relative to the control, a buffered nanoalloy will exhibit less grain growth after high-temperature exposure.
Relative to the control, a buffered nanoalloy will better retain a uniform elemental distribution after high-temperature exposure.
The cited Fe- and Mn-containing rocksalt high-entropy oxide has improved structural robustness.
The prediction is limited to application-relevant high-temperature conditions and may fail far below or above that regime because other kinetic or thermodynamic factors may dominate.
The quantitative benefit of buffering and its sensitivity to elemental selection in nanoalloys are not established.
A lack of statistically significant improvement in segregation, grain growth, or decomposition relative to the control would falsify the proposed governing role of the buffering sublattice.
